5. Dictionary encoding and the RLE/bit-packing hybrid

Plain encoding writes values back to back: 8 bytes per 64-bit integer, and for strings a 4-byte length followed by the bytes. That is why event_type takes 9.36 MB plain: one million strings averaging about 5 characters, plus 4 bytes of length each.

Dictionary encoding collects the distinct values of the column chunk into a dictionary page and replaces each value with its index. event_type has 8 distinct values, so the dictionary is 8 short strings and the data pages hold one million indices between 0 and 7. Those indices are then stored with Parquet's RLE/bit-packing hybrid encoding (the specification calls the combination RLE_DICTIONARY). Bit-packing stores each index in the fewest bits that can hold the largest: 8 values need 3 bits (23 = 8), so one million indices take 3,000,000 bits = 375,000 bytes. The measured column is 379,818 bytes — 375,000 for the codes plus the dictionary and page headers. country, with 50 values, needs 6 bits (26 = 64 ≥ 50): 750,000 bytes predicted, 754,766 measured. The arithmetic is exact because the encoding is that simple.

The RLE (run-length encoding) half of the hybrid kicks in when the same index repeats: instead of bit-packing 400 copies of "2", it writes "2, repeated 400 times" in a couple of bytes. In our file the event types are in random order, so runs are short and bit-packing does all the work. When the same table is sorted by event_type and then country, the event_type column becomes 8 long runs and shrinks from 380 KB to 2.9 KB; country becomes 400 runs (50 per event type) and shrinks to 3.9 KB.

Dictionary encoding has a limit. The dictionary itself must fit in its page limit (1 MB by default in both pyarrow and parquet-java). event_id is unique: its dictionary would need a million entries, so after the first ~131,000 values (1 MB ÷ 8 bytes) the writer gives up — dictionary fallback — and writes the rest of the chunk in plain encoding. The footer records both encodings (PLAIN, RLE, RLE_DICTIONARY), and the column ends up slightly larger than plain (8.27 MB versus 8.00 MB) because of the wasted dictionary. user_id, with 200,000 distinct values, also overflows its dictionary partway through. High-cardinality columns are where general-purpose compression has to do the work instead.

6. Delta encoding for ordered numbers

Some columns are neither repetitive nor random: they are ordered. event_id increases by exactly 1 per row; ts increases by an average of 86 milliseconds. Storing each value in 8 bytes wastes almost all of the bits. Delta encoding (DELTA_BINARY_PACKED in Parquet) stores the first value, then the differences between consecutive values, in blocks; within each block it subtracts the smallest difference and bit-packs the remainders. For event_id every difference is 1, so every remainder is 0 and needs 0 bits: writing this column with delta encoding produced 24,000 bytes instead of 8,000,000 — essentially just block headers. For ts, gaps range from 0 to a few hundred milliseconds, needing around 9 bits each: 1.17 MB instead of 8 MB, uncompressed. pyarrow does not choose delta encoding by default; you request it per column with column_encoding={"ts": "DELTA_BINARY_PACKED"} and use_dictionary turned off for that column. Spark's parquet-java writer uses delta encodings automatically only for the newer "v2" data pages.

Parquet has other encodings for specific shapes: DELTA_LENGTH_BYTE_ARRAY and DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY for strings (the latter stores shared prefixes once, which suits sorted URLs or keys), and BYTE_STREAM_SPLIT for floating-point numbers, which writes all the first bytes of the values, then all the second bytes and so on. Floats rarely repeat exactly, but their high-order bytes (sign and exponent) are very similar, so splitting them out gives the compression codec long runs of similar bytes. Uber reported in 2022 that byte-stream split alone does not shrink data but improves what a codec achieves afterwards.

7. Nulls and definition levels

How does Parquet store price, which is null on 90% of rows? It does not store the nulls as values. Alongside each optional column it stores definition levels: for a flat optional column, one small number per row, 1 if the value is present and 0 if it is null, encoded with the same RLE/bit-packing hybrid (1 bit per row, with long runs of zeros collapsing). The value stream then holds only the 100,000 real prices. Plain, that is 100,000 × 8 bytes = 800 KB plus about 125 KB of 1-bit levels, which matches the measured 0.96 MB; with dictionary encoding (many prices repeat at two decimal places) it drops to 0.40 MB. Nested data (lists and structs) adds repetition levels that record where each list begins — the Dremel idea db12 described — but you rarely need to think about them unless you are debugging a writer.

8. Compression codecs

After encoding, each page can be compressed with a general-purpose codec. The common ones are Snappy (very fast, modest ratio; the default in pyarrow and in Spark's Parquet writer), zstd (Zstandard: much better ratio at modest CPU cost, with levels 1 to 22), gzip (good ratio, slow to decompress), and LZ4 (very fast). Codecs work on bytes, finding repeated byte sequences, so they help most on what encodings left behind. The measured table shows it: Snappy halves the integer and timestamp columns, which still contain long runs of identical high-order bytes, but does nothing for event_type and country, which bit-packing already squeezed to near their information content (Snappy even added a few hundred bytes of framing). zstd goes much further on integers — event_id 1.28 MB versus Snappy's 4.28 MB — because it finds longer-range patterns.

Because compression is per page, a reader decompresses only the pages it reads, and pages from different columns can be decoded in parallel. Decompression speed matters more than compression speed for tables that are written once and read many times; zstd decompresses fast at any level, which is why many lakes moved to it. The trade-off is write-time CPU: high zstd levels are slow to compress.

9. Statistics and predicate pushdown

Every column chunk's metadata in the footer can carry statistics: minimum value, maximum value and null count. Writers can also add a page index — a ColumnIndex with min and max per page and an OffsetIndex with each page's location — so a reader can skip individual pages, not just whole row groups. (pyarrow writes chunk statistics by default but the page index only when you pass write_page_index=True.) Optionally a writer adds a Bloom filter per column chunk: a compact bit array that can say "this value is definitely not in this chunk", useful for equality lookups on high-cardinality columns like IDs. parquet-java leaves Bloom filters off by default.

Predicate pushdown is the engine passing a query's filter down to the reader. Suppose the same one million events are written with 10 row groups of 100,000 rows, sorted by time, and a query asks for WHERE ts >= '12:00' AND ts < '13:00'. The footer (7.6 KB for this file, versus 1.4 KB for the one-row-group file) lists each row group's ts range. Measured:

Row groupmin tsmax tsRead?
0 – 300:00:0009:36:47skip

Two of ten row groups survive, and of those only the columns in the SELECT are fetched (column projection). If the query selects event_type and country, the reader fetches about 2/10 of their 1.1 MB plus the ts chunks needed to apply the filter exactly — perhaps 1.2 MB of a 15 MB file. The engine still applies the filter row by row inside the surviving row groups; statistics only tell it what it can safely ignore.

This is the most important practical fact about statistics: they describe the data, they do not organise it. Sort order is a choice the writer makes, and choosing it trades one column's pushdown and compression against another's. When the measured table was sorted by event_type and country, those two columns shrank to almost nothing, but ts grew from 4.58 MB to 5.61 MB and event_id from 4.28 MB to 4.89 MB (Snappy), the file as a whole grew from 15.1 MB to 15.6 MB, and the time filter above would no longer skip anything. de3 covers how to choose, and techniques such as Z-ordering that cluster on several columns at once.

10. ORC in one section

ORC (Optimized Row Columnar) came from the Hive project at about the same time as Parquet and has the same core ideas with different names. A file is divided into stripes (64 MB by default) instead of row groups; within each stripe, columns are stored as streams; every 10,000 rows (the row index stride) ORC records min/max and positions, giving page-like skipping built in; and the file and stripe footers hold metadata. ORC has rich encodings and optional Bloom filters, and the current ORC documentation lists zstd as the default codec. ORC remains strong in Hive- and Trino-heavy shops; Parquet won broader ecosystem support (Spark's default, pandas, Arrow, DuckDB, every warehouse's external tables, every table format), so new platforms usually standardise on Parquet.

11. The small-files problem

Everything above assumed reasonably large files. Real lakes often have the opposite. A streaming job that commits every minute, a Spark job with 2,000 tasks each writing its own file into each of 50 partitions, a pipeline that appends one file per incoming API call — each produces thousands or millions of small files. Each file carries fixed costs that do not shrink with its size:

  • Listing: object stores return at most 1,000 keys per list request (S3's ListObjectsV2 limit), so 1,000,000 files need 1,000 sequential-ish list calls before planning can even begin — unless a table format's metadata already lists them (de4).
  • Opening: at least one request to read the footer and one or more for data, each with tens of milliseconds of first-byte latency on object storage.
  • Scheduling: engines such as Spark create read tasks from files and byte ranges; with tiny files, task launch overhead (tens of milliseconds each) dominates. Spark mitigates this by packing small files together into one task, treating each file as costing an extra 4 MB (spark.sql.files.openCostInBytes) when packing up to 128 MB per task (spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes).
  • Worse files: a 1 MB Parquet file has one tiny row group, little for dictionaries and codecs to find, a footer proportionally large, and statistics that are fine-grained but must be read separately for each file.
  • Metadata: catalogs, table-format manifests and (on HDFS) the NameNode's memory all grow with file count.

Size it. One day of events, 100 GB after encoding. As 100,000 files of 1 MB, a full scan needs about 100 list calls, at least 200,000 GET requests (footer plus data per file), and — even at 200 concurrent requests and 30 ms each — about 30 seconds of pure request latency before counting any data transfer; Spark plans tens of thousands of tasks. As 800 files of 128 MB, it needs one list call, about 1,600 GETs plus ranged reads within files, and a few hundred tasks. The bytes read are the same; the overhead differs by two orders of magnitude. At the request price (S3 Standard GETs are fractions of a cent per thousand), the money is small; the time and the planning overhead are not.

The cures are on both sides. On write: buffer longer before committing, repartition or coalesce before writing so each task writes one file per output partition, and size output files deliberately (many writers have a target file size option). After write: compaction, a maintenance job that rewrites small files into large ones — safe only when a table format commits the swap atomically, which de3 and de4 build on. A common target is files of 128 MB to 1 GB, with row groups of 64–256 MB inside them so a large file still splits into parallel read tasks.
deep:
Why columnar plus vectorised reading is a CPU story, not just an I/O story

Bytes saved on disk are obvious; less obvious is that columnar files also make the CPU faster. When a reader decodes a page, it produces a batch of thousands of values of one type laid out contiguously in memory — the Apache Arrow in-memory format is the common target. The engine then runs tight loops over those arrays: compare every timestamp in the batch to the filter bound, producing a bitmap; sum every price where the bitmap is set. Such loops use SIMD instructions (one instruction operating on 4–16 values) and stay in the CPU cache. A row format forces the engine to walk record by record, branching on each field. This is why Spark's vectorized Parquet reader (on by default) and engines like DuckDB are so much faster than row-at-a-time readers even on cached data. It is also why dictionary-encoded columns can sometimes be filtered without decoding: compare the filter to the 8 dictionary entries once, then scan the 3-bit codes.

Statistics have sharp edges

Min/max statistics are only useful if the reader trusts them, and there have been real bugs. Early Parquet writers computed string min/max with signed byte comparison, which is wrong for non-ASCII UTF-8, so readers learned to ignore string statistics from old writer versions; Parquet later added a ColumnOrder field to the footer and new min_value/max_value fields with defined ordering. Long strings make statistics large, so writers truncate them (parquet-java's column-index truncate length is 64 bytes); a truncated max must be rounded up so it is still an upper bound. Floating-point NaN breaks ordering and is handled specially. The practical lesson: when a pushdown that should work does not, inspect the footer — statistics may be missing, truncated, or deliberately ignored for that writer version.

Choosing row-group and file sizes is a three-way trade

Row groups trade pushdown granularity, memory and parallelism. A row group is buffered in memory by the writer until it is flushed (so a 1 GB row group across 200 columns needs a lot of writer memory), is the finest unit a reader can skip with chunk statistics, and is typically the unit of parallel splitting when an engine divides one big file across tasks. Very large row groups give long sequential reads and good compression but coarse skipping and few splits; very small ones give fine skipping but many seeks and a large footer. The page index loosens the trade by allowing page-level skipping inside large row groups. For object storage, where each request costs tens of milliseconds, the practical sweet spot is files of hundreds of megabytes with row groups of roughly 64–256 MB; for a training data loader doing random access, smaller row groups (or a dedicated shard format, de12) are better.

Schema evolution at the file level, and why IDs beat names

Each Parquet file carries its own schema, so a table made of many files may contain several schema versions. Engines reconcile them by matching column names: a new nullable column reads as null in old files; a dropped column is ignored. Renames are the trap: if price is renamed to unit_price, old files have price and new ones unit_price, and a by-name reader sees two half-empty columns. Iceberg solves this by writing a numeric field ID into each Parquet column's schema and resolving by ID, so a rename is a metadata-only change and old files still map correctly. Type changes are harder: widening int to long can be read safely; anything else usually means rewriting data. Avro sidesteps much of this with explicit reader/writer schema resolution and aliases. This is one of the main reasons de4's table formats exist.

Formats for ML data are under pressure

Parquet was designed for analytical scans, and ML workloads stress it in new ways. Training tables can have thousands of feature columns, making footers megabytes long and metadata parsing a real cost. Embedding columns are fixed-length float vectors that compress poorly and are better stored as fixed-size lists with byte-stream split. Data loaders want random access to individual rows for shuffling, which row-group-oriented files serve badly. Newer formats such as Lance (built around fast random access and vector search) and research formats like Nimble (from Meta, aimed at very wide tables) target these needs; the common practical response is still Parquet with tuned row groups for preprocessing, then conversion into training shards (de12). It is worth knowing the pressures exist, and being able to explain them, rather than knowing every new format's name.

Encryption and integrity

Parquet supports modular encryption: the footer and individual columns can be encrypted with different keys, so a table can expose non-sensitive columns to everyone while only principals with the right key decrypt, say, an email column. Pages can also carry CRC checksums (pyarrow's write_page_checksum, off by default) to detect corruption. Both are worth knowing because ML feature tables frequently mix sensitive and non-sensitive columns, and silent corruption in a training set is otherwise invisible.
prod:
How file formats hurt in production

The JSON-forever bronze layer. Raw JSON is landed "temporarily" and never converted; analysts query it directly. Symptom: queries whose cost and runtime scale with total history, frequent parse failures, and type confusion (the same field as string in some files and number in others). Fix: convert to typed Parquet in silver with schema enforcement, and quarantine records that do not parse.

Small files from streaming and over-partitioned writes. Symptom: Spark jobs whose driver spends minutes planning, tens of thousands of tiny tasks each running for milliseconds, slow listings, a table-format metadata tree that keeps growing. Check file count and median file size per partition; a median under 32 MB is a red flag. Fix: coalesce or repartition before writing, longer trigger intervals, scheduled compaction.

Pushdown that silently stopped working. Symptom: a query that used to read a few gigabytes reads terabytes, after a writer change. Causes: a new writer that omits statistics, timestamps written as strings, a lost sort order, or a filter wrapped in a function (WHERE date(ts) = …) that the reader cannot push down. Check the query's "files read / bytes read" metrics and the footers of new files.

Precision and type drift. Timestamps written as INT96 (a legacy Impala/Hive encoding) by one writer and as INT64 microseconds by another; decimals written as doubles; integers that overflowed because a source widened its column. These show up as subtly wrong values in features, not as errors. Fix: pin types in the data contract and test new files against it.

Dictionary blow-up and memory. Writers buffering a whole row group of a very wide table can run out of memory; readers decoding large dictionaries for many columns at once can too. Symptom: writer OOM on wide feature tables. Fix: smaller row groups for wide tables, fewer columns per file, or splitting the table.

Tools and metrics

pyarrow.parquet.ParquetFile(path).metadata (used in the lab) and the parquet-cli tool from parquet-java print row groups, column chunk sizes, encodings, codecs and statistics. Query engines report files and bytes scanned per query — the single most useful number for spotting a format or layout problem. Track per table: file count, median and p10 file size, bytes per row, and compression ratio over time.

The case: Uber's file-format cost work (2022)

In "Cost Efficiency @ Scale in Big Data File Format" (Uber Engineering blog, 25 January 2022, by Xinli Shang, Zheng Shao and Mohammad Islam), Uber describes reducing storage in its Parquet-dominated lake by changing how files are written, not what they contain. Before the project, the lake mainly used gzip and Snappy. On their ten largest Hive tables with zstd at the default level 3, they measured about 7% less storage than gzip, about 39% less than Snappy, and about 79% less than uncompressed. Read cost did not suffer: in their query benchmarks zstd's vCore-seconds were close to Snappy's on a full scan and much lower on queries with shuffles, filters and aggregations, because less data was read and moved. Testing levels 1 to 22 on 65 one-gigabyte files, they found size gains flattened while write time kept rising, and chose level 19 only for one-off offline conversion of existing gzip data.

They also contributed tooling upstream: zstd support in parquet-java that no longer depended on Hadoop's native library (PARQUET-1866, in Parquet 1.12.0), a "trans-compression" command to recompress existing files without decoding the data (PARQUET-1949), and a column-pruning tool that copies files while skipping unused columns about 20 times faster than rewriting them with Spark (PARQUET-1800), after identifying unused columns from lineage and query audit logs. And they measured sort order: on one table with a UUID, a timestamp and latitude/longitude, sorting rows by UUID then time cut data size by 32%. Every idea in this lesson — codec choice, column removal, sort order — was worth petabytes at their scale.
myths: Parquet is compressed, so the codec is what makes it small.

Most of the saving comes from encoding before any codec runs. In the measured example, dictionary and bit-packing alone shrink the event_type column from 9.4 MB of plain strings to 0.38 MB, and Snappy then adds nothing. Codecs help most on columns that encodings cannot simplify, such as high-cardinality IDs and free text.
Bigger row groups are always better.

Larger row groups mean fewer footer entries, longer sequential reads and better compression, but they also mean coarser statistics (one min/max covers more rows, so less can be skipped), more memory for writers that buffer a whole row group, and fewer units of parallelism when a file is split across tasks. 128 MB to 1 GB is a common range; the right value depends on how the data is filtered and read.
Predicate pushdown means Parquet has an index.

Plain Parquet has min/max statistics per column chunk (and optionally per page) and optional Bloom filters, not a B-tree. Statistics only help when values are clustered, so that each row group covers a narrow range. On randomly ordered data every row group's min and max span nearly the whole domain and nothing is skipped — which is why sort order (de3) matters as much as the format.
CSV is fine for a lake because every tool reads it.

Every tool reads it differently. CSV has no types, no standard for nulls, quoting or encodings, and no schema; a single unescaped comma or newline in a text field shifts every following column. It must be fully parsed to read even one column, and it cannot be split safely when fields may contain newlines. Keep CSV at the edges (partner drops, exports) and convert to Parquet in bronze or silver.
Avro and Parquet compete; pick one.

They are built for different jobs. Avro is row-oriented with the schema in the file header and is ideal for writing one record at a time, for messages in Kafka and for pipelines that read whole records. Parquet is columnar and ideal for analytical scans of a few columns. Many platforms use Avro (or Protobuf) in motion and Parquet at rest.
lab:
Goal: write a real Parquet file and read its anatomy and statistics yourself. Uses pandas and pyarrow from C:\ra_projects\how-to-train-your-gpt\gpt_env (pyarrow 25); about 15 minutes.

  1. Build a table of 1,000,000 rows with NumPy: event_id as np.arange, ts as sorted random milliseconds within one day, user_id as random integers up to 200,000, event_type chosen from 8 strings with uneven probabilities, country from 50 codes. Convert with pa.table({...}).
  2. Write it three ways with pq.write_table: compression="none", "snappy" and "zstd"; also write it as CSV with pyarrow.csv.write_csv. Print os.path.getsize for each.
  3. Open the Snappy file with md = pq.ParquetFile(path).metadata. For each column, print md.row_group(0).column(i).encodings, total_uncompressed_size, total_compressed_size and the statistics min/max.
  4. Rewrite with row_group_size=100_000, print each row group's ts min and max, then read with pq.read_table(path, columns=["event_type"], filters=[("ts", ">=", t12), ("ts", "<", t13)]).
  5. Try next: shuffle the rows before writing (table.take(np.random.permutation(n))) and print the row-group ranges again.

What to look for. CSV should be roughly 3–4 times the Snappy file. event_type's encoded size should be close to 1,000,000 × 3 bits = 375 KB, and country's close to 750 KB — the bit-packing arithmetic made visible. event_id's encodings should list both RLE_DICTIONARY and PLAIN: the dictionary fallback. With 10 sorted row groups, each ts range covers about 2.4 hours, so the filter can skip eight of them; after shuffling, every range spans the whole day and nothing can be skipped.
recap: CSV and JSON are text, untyped and row-oriented, so readers must parse every byte of every row; they are fragile at scale and several times larger than binary columnar files.

Avro is a compact binary row format with its schema in the file header and sync markers between blocks; it suits streaming, messages and whole-record reads, and supports schema evolution through reader and writer schemas.

A Parquet file holds row groups; each row group holds one column chunk per column; each column chunk holds pages; the footer at the end lists every row group and column chunk with offsets, sizes, encodings and statistics.

Encodings do most of the work: dictionary encoding replaces repeated values with small integer codes, the RLE/bit-packing hybrid stores those codes in the minimum number of bits and collapses runs, and delta encoding stores differences between neighbouring integers.
In the measured example, one million events took 56.3 MB as CSV, about 140 MB as JSON lines, 25.9 MB as uncompressed Parquet, 15.1 MB with Snappy and 7.9 MB with Zstandard.
Statistics (min, max, null count) per column chunk and optionally per page let readers skip row groups and pages that cannot match a filter, but only if the data is clustered on the filtered column.
Readers read the footer first, then fetch only the byte ranges of the columns and row groups they need, which on object storage turns a scan into a few large ranged GET requests.

The small-files problem is per-file overhead — listing, opening, reading footers and scheduling a task per file — multiplied by thousands of files, plus poor compression and statistics in each tiny file; the cure is fewer, larger files (roughly 128 MB to 1 GB) via better writes and compaction.
glossary: Avro
An Apache binary, row-oriented serialisation format whose files carry their schema in a header; widely used for Kafka messages and pipeline records.
Bit-packing
Storing small integers using only as many bits as the largest one needs, e.g. 3 bits each for codes 0–7 instead of 32 or 64.
Bloom filter
A compact probabilistic structure that answers "definitely not present" or "possibly present" for a value; Parquet can store one per column chunk to skip chunks on equality filters.
BYTE_STREAM_SPLIT

A Parquet encoding for floating-point (and some fixed-width) values that writes the first byte of every value, then every second byte, and so on, so a following compression codec finds more repetition.
Codec
A general-purpose compression algorithm applied to encoded pages, such as Snappy, Zstandard (zstd), gzip or LZ4.
Column chunk
The data of one column inside one row group of a Parquet file, stored contiguously and made of pages.
Column projection
Reading only the columns a query references; in columnar formats it means not fetching the other columns' bytes at all.
Compaction
Rewriting many small files into fewer large ones, usually as a scheduled maintenance job.
CSV
Comma-separated values: a plain-text format with one record per line and fields separated by commas, with no types or standard null handling.
Definition level
Per-value metadata in Parquet saying how much of an optional (or nested) field's path is present; for a flat optional column it simply marks null versus not null.
Delta encoding
Storing each value as the difference from the previous one (DELTA_BINARY_PACKED in Parquet), so sorted or slowly changing integers and timestamps become tiny numbers.
Dictionary encoding
Storing each distinct value once in a dictionary and replacing every occurrence with its integer position in the dictionary.
Dictionary fallback
When a column's dictionary grows past its size limit (1 MB by default in parquet-java and pyarrow), the writer stops dictionary-encoding the rest of that column chunk and writes plain values.
Footer
The metadata block at the end of a Parquet file (FileMetaData, serialised with Thrift) followed by its 4-byte length and the magic bytes PAR1.
INT96
A legacy 12-byte Parquet timestamp encoding written by old Impala and Hive versions; modern writers use 64-bit integers with an explicit unit instead.
JSON lines
A text format with one JSON object per line; common for logs and event exports.
ORC
Optimized Row Columnar: an Apache columnar format from the Hive ecosystem, organised in stripes with lightweight indexes; similar in purpose to Parquet.
Page

The smallest unit of encoding and compression in Parquet, typically around 1 MB or 20,000 rows by default in common writers; data pages hold values, a dictionary page holds a column chunk's dictionary.
Page index
Optional Parquet structures (ColumnIndex and OffsetIndex) that store min/max per page and page locations, letting readers skip pages, not just row groups.
Parquet
An Apache open columnar file format for analytics: row groups, column chunks and pages, with encodings, compression and statistics.
Predicate pushdown
Passing a query's filter down to the file reader so it can skip row groups or pages whose statistics prove no row can match.
RLE (run-length encoding)
Storing a run of identical values as (value, count); Parquet's RLE/bit-packing hybrid switches between runs and bit-packed groups.
Row group
A horizontal slice of a Parquet file's rows; within it each column is stored as a separate column chunk.
Schema evolution
Changing a dataset's schema over time (adding, removing, renaming or retyping fields) while old and new data stay readable.
SIMD
Single instruction, multiple data: CPU instructions that apply one operation to a short vector of values at once, which columnar batches make easy to use.
Small-files problem
The slowdown and cost caused by datasets made of very many small files, where per-file overhead dominates the actual data reading.
Snappy
A fast compression codec from Google with a modest compression ratio; the default Parquet codec in pyarrow and Spark.
Splittable
A file that can be divided into pieces processed independently by different tasks, which needs boundaries a reader can find (row groups, stripes, sync markers).
Statistics
Per-column-chunk (and optionally per-page) metadata such as minimum, maximum and null count, used for skipping data.
Stripe
ORC's equivalent of a row group: a horizontal slice of rows, 64 MB by default, with its own index and footer.
Sync marker
A random 16-byte value repeated between blocks of an Avro file so a reader starting mid-file can find the next block boundary.
Thrift
A serialisation framework (originally from Facebook) that Parquet uses to encode its metadata structures.
Zstandard (zstd)
A modern compression codec with tunable levels that typically compresses much better than Snappy at moderate CPU cost, and decompresses quickly.
drill:
Diagnose: the 40-minute feature query

A nightly feature job computes, for each user, purchase counts over the last 7 days from a table silver.events. The table is 90 days of Parquet in S3, 300 GB in total, partitioned by date (one folder per day). The query filters event_type = 'purchase' and the last 7 days. It used to take 4 minutes; it now takes 40. The Spark UI shows it reads all 7 partitions fully: 23 GB, 240,000 files, 240,000 tasks. A month ago an upstream team switched landing from hourly batches to a streaming job with a 10-second trigger. What happened, and what do you change?

Answer

Diagnosis. The date filter works (7 of 90 partitions), but inside each day there are now about 34,000 files (240,000 ÷ 7), averaging about 100 KB each (23 GB ÷ 240,000). That is the streaming job: one file per task per trigger. With 8,640 ten-second triggers a day and a handful of tasks per trigger, tens of thousands of files a day is exactly what to expect. The job is dominated by per-file overhead: listing, a footer read and a data read per file, and task scheduling — 240,000 tasks at even 10 ms of overhead each is 40 minutes of task time before any real work. The tiny files also kill pushdown: each holds a few seconds of mixed event types, so per-file statistics for event_type span many values, and every file must be opened just to learn that.

Fix in the short term. Compact each day into files of roughly 256 MB–1 GB: 23 GB ÷ 7 ≈ 3.3 GB per day becomes about 4–13 files per day. Sort within each compacted file by event_type then ts, so the purchase rows (about 2% of events) sit in a few row groups and the others are skipped from statistics. Run compaction daily (or hourly for the current day) as a maintenance job, and use a table format so the swap is atomic and readers never see duplicates.

Fix in the long term. Make the streaming writer coalesce its output (fewer tasks writing, a longer trigger such as one minute if freshness allows) and give the landing table a file-count and median-file-size check with an alert. Expected result: the 7-day read becomes about 30–90 files and, with sorting, reads well under 1 GB — back to a few minutes or less.
qa: E
Why is Parquet so much smaller and faster to query than CSV for the same data?

Three reasons stack. Parquet is binary and typed, so a 64-bit integer takes at most 8 bytes rather than up to 20 characters plus a delimiter. It is columnar, so similar values sit together and encodings such as dictionary, run-length and delta collapse them before a codec even runs. And it carries metadata — schema, offsets, statistics — so a reader fetches only the columns and row groups it needs instead of parsing every byte. In the measured one-million-event example, CSV was 56 MB and Parquet with zstd was 7.9 MB, and a query on two columns reads a fraction of that.
E
Describe the physical layout of a Parquet file.

A file starts with the 4 magic bytes PAR1, then one or more row groups, each a horizontal slice of rows. Inside a row group each column is a contiguous column chunk, and each column chunk is a sequence of pages — an optional dictionary page followed by data pages that are encoded and compressed independently. At the end is the footer: Thrift-encoded metadata with the schema and, for every row group and column chunk, its offset, size, encodings and statistics, followed by a 4-byte footer length and PAR1 again. Readers read the end first, then jump to exactly the byte ranges they need.
E
When would you choose Avro over Parquet?

When records are written one at a time and read whole: Kafka messages, CDC events, RPC payloads, or a landing format for a streaming pipeline. Avro is a compact binary row format, writes are cheap appends, the schema travels in the file header (or in a schema registry for messages), and its reader/writer schema resolution makes evolution safe. For analytical scans of a few columns over many rows, convert to Parquet.
M
Explain dictionary encoding and the RLE/bit-packing hybrid with numbers.

Dictionary encoding stores each distinct value once and replaces every value with its index. A column of one million event types with 8 distinct values becomes an 8-entry dictionary plus one million codes from 0 to 7. Those codes need only 3 bits each, so bit-packing stores them in about 375 KB instead of millions of bytes of strings, and when the same code repeats in a run (as it does if data is sorted) RLE stores the run as one value and a count. Measured with pyarrow, the column went from 9.4 MB plain to 380 KB, and to under 3 KB once the data was sorted by event type.

Follow-up: When does dictionary encoding stop helping? — When cardinality is high: the dictionary grows past its page limit (1 MB by default in parquet-java and pyarrow) and the writer falls back to plain encoding for the rest of the chunk, as it did for unique event IDs.
M
What is predicate pushdown and when does it fail to help?

The engine passes the filter down to the file reader, which compares it with the min and max statistics of each row group (and, with a page index, each page) and skips any whose range cannot contain a match. It helps only when data is clustered on the filtered column, so each row group covers a narrow range — for example a file sorted by timestamp queried for one hour. On randomly ordered data every row group spans nearly the whole range of values, statistics prove nothing, and the reader reads everything. It also fails for filters on expressions the reader cannot evaluate against statistics, such as a function applied to the column.

Follow-up: How do you get pushdown to work for an ID lookup? — Sort or cluster by the ID so ranges are narrow, or write Bloom filters for that column so equality lookups can skip chunks that definitely lack the value.
M
Snappy or zstd for Parquet in a data lake? Justify with numbers.

Usually zstd at a low-to-moderate level for data at rest. In the measured example Snappy produced 15.1 MB and zstd 7.9 MB from the same 25.9 MB of encoded data; Uber reported about 39% less storage moving its largest tables from Snappy to zstd, with lower vCore-seconds on most queries because less data was read and shuffled. Snappy remains a fine choice for short-lived intermediate data where write CPU dominates. Decompression speed is similar enough that read-heavy tables benefit from the smaller size.

Follow-up: Should you just use the highest zstd level? — No: write time rises steeply with level while size gains flatten; Uber found no benefit past level 19 even for one-off offline conversion, and for routine writes levels around 1 to 3 are the usual default.
M
What is the small-files problem and how big does it get?

Every file costs a listing entry, at least one request to read its footer and another for its data, task-scheduling overhead in engines that create a task per file, and metadata in the catalog or table format; small files also compress worse and have less useful statistics. A day of 100 GB stored as 100,000 one-megabyte files means about 200,000 GET requests and 100,000 tasks, where 800 files of 128 MB would need about 1,600 requests and a few hundred tasks. The fix is to write fewer, larger files (buffer longer, repartition before writing) and compact regularly.

Follow-up: Why does a streaming job create so many small files? — It commits output every trigger interval per output partition and per task, so a 10-second trigger, 50 tasks and 24 hourly partitions can produce hundreds of thousands of files a day unless output is coalesced or compacted.
M
How does a reader read only two columns of a 1 GB Parquet file on S3?

It issues a ranged GET for the tail of the file to read the footer length and footer (often by speculatively reading the last 64 KB or so, which usually contains the whole footer). From the footer it knows the byte offset and length of each column chunk in each row group, applies any statistics-based skipping, and then issues ranged GETs only for the two needed column chunks per surviving row group, often coalescing nearby ranges. The other columns' bytes are never transferred.
M
How does schema evolution work in Avro versus Parquet?

Avro resolves a writer's schema against the reader's schema field by field by name: added fields need a default so old data can be read, removed fields are ignored, and type promotions such as int to long are allowed. Parquet files each carry their own schema; engines either take one file's schema or merge schemas across files, and columns are matched by name (or by field ID when written by Iceberg). Adding nullable columns is easy in both; renames and type changes are where things break, which is why table formats track column IDs (de4).
H
A dashboard query filtering one user_id over a 2 TB Parquet table reads all 2 TB. Why, and what would you change?

user_id values are spread randomly across files and row groups, so every row group's min/max covers nearly the full ID range and statistics skip nothing. Options: cluster or sort the data by user_id (or Z-order on user_id plus date, de3) so ranges become narrow; write Bloom filters on user_id so equality lookups skip chunks that cannot contain the ID; enable page indexes for finer skipping; or, if point lookups dominate, serve them from a key-value store and keep Parquet for scans. I would measure files and row groups read before and after each change.

Follow-up: What does sorting by user_id cost? — Other columns that were naturally ordered, such as timestamps, compress worse once their order is destroyed; in the measured example sorting by type and country grew the timestamp column from 4.6 MB to 5.6 MB, and a time-range filter loses its pushdown.
H
Design the file layout for a 5 TB/day event stream that is landed every five minutes but queried mostly by day and event type.

Land micro-batches as Parquet with zstd into an hourly bronze area and accept small files there. Run a compaction job (hourly or daily) that rewrites each hour or day into files of roughly 256 MB to 1 GB, sorted by event_type and then timestamp, so dictionary/RLE collapse the type column and statistics prune on type and time. With 5 TB/day of encoded output and 512 MB files, that is about 10,000 files a day instead of hundreds of thousands. Use a table format so compaction swaps files atomically, and keep row groups around 128 MB so a large file still splits into parallel tasks.

Follow-up: How do readers avoid seeing both the small files and the compacted copy during the rewrite? — The table format commits the compaction as one snapshot that removes the small files and adds the large ones, so readers see one version or the other (de4).
H
Your Spark job reading Parquet got 5× slower after an upstream team changed their writer. File count and total size are unchanged. What might they have changed?

Look at the footers. Possibilities: they disabled statistics or switched to a writer that writes no page index, so pushdown stopped skipping; they changed the sort order, so row-group ranges widened; they grew row groups to the whole file, so the file can no longer be split into several tasks and parallelism dropped; they switched codec (gzip is slower to decompress than Snappy or zstd); or they changed types — timestamps as strings or decimals as strings disable both efficient encodings and comparisons. parquet-tools or pyarrow's metadata API will show row-group counts, encodings, codecs and statistics side by side.

Follow-up: What would you put in the data contract to prevent this? — Required codec, target file and row-group sizes, sort columns, statistics enabled and column types, all checked automatically on new files (de11).

t: Partitioning and layout: partition pruning, too many vs too few partitions, bucketing, sort order, Z-order and Hilbert clustering, compaction
sum: How the arrangement of files decides how much a query reads: Hive-style partition directories and pruning, choosing partition columns and the arithmetic of too many or too few partitions, bucketing for shuffle-free joins, sort order and file statistics, multi-column clustering with Z-order and Hilbert curves worked by hand, compaction, and Salesforce's move from 4 million tiny files to Z-ordered Delta tables.
prereq: de2

Parquet stores min/max statistics per row group and column; readers skip data whose ranges cannot match a filter, but only if the data is clustered on that column; many small files cost far more to read than a few large ones.
de1
A lake keeps tables as files in object storage; bronze, silver and gold layers are rewritten by batch jobs.
db12
Analytical queries filter and aggregate over a few columns of many rows, and zone maps and partition pruning let an engine skip whole blocks.
sc18
Batch jobs shuffle data by key between stages; skew means one key holds far more data than the others.
why:
A B2B software company stores every customer "engagement" — an email opened, a link clicked — in a lake table, and wants each customer organisation's data to be easy to find and easy to delete. So it partitions the table by organisation and by day: one directory per org per date. It sounds tidy. But 90% of the organisations are small and produce a few thousand engagements a day — a few hundred kilobytes. Every org-day directory gets its own files, and those files are tiny: a sampled partition has 175 files of about 7 KB each. The table reaches more than four million files. Running a batch of 200,000 updates now takes over eight hours, because every update has to find, open and rewrite files across thousands of directories.

This is a real story, told by Salesforce engineering in 2020, and its punchline is that nothing was wrong with the data, the engine or the hardware. The table's layout — how rows were divided into directories and files and in what order — was wrong for the data's shape. The fix was a different layout: partition only by organisation, cluster the rows inside each partition by date, and keep files in a sensible size range. A batch of 25 million updates and deletes then finished in 15 minutes.

de2 showed that a single Parquet file can skip most of its bytes if its rows are well ordered. This lesson steps up a level to the whole table: how rows are divided into partitions, how they are ordered within files, how two tables can be laid out so a join needs no network shuffle, and how to keep the layout healthy as small writes keep arriving. For ML, layout decides whether a feature backfill over two years reads 2 TB or 200 TB, whether a training-set join runs in minutes or hours, and whether a GDPR deletion request is a quick rewrite or a week-long job.

You will learn Hive-style partitioning and pruning, how to choose partition columns with numbers for too many and too few partitions, how writers decide how many files they create, bucketing for joins, sort order and its effect on statistics, multi-column clustering with Z-order and Hilbert curves worked out by hand, and compaction — then the Salesforce case in detail.
primer:
The mental model: a library

A library with a million books has to decide how to arrange them. The first decision is which rooms to put books in: fiction in one room, science in another, history in a third. A reader looking for a chemistry book walks straight into the science room and ignores the rest of the building. That is partitioning, and walking past the other rooms is partition pruning.

The second decision is the order of books on the shelves within each room. If science books are shelved alphabetically by author, a reader looking for a particular author goes to one shelf; a reader looking for every book about chemistry must check every shelf. Shelve by subject instead and the chemistry reader goes to one bay, while the author search gets hard. That is sort order: whichever key you sort by gets fast lookups, and other keys do not.

Too many rooms is a real failure. If the library makes a separate room for every author, there are a hundred thousand rooms, most holding two books; readers spend their day opening doors. Too few rooms (one giant hall) means every reader searches everything. The useful middle is a few dozen rooms, each large enough to be worth having, with sensible shelving inside.

A clever librarian can also shelve by two things at once — not perfectly by either, but well enough by both — by grouping books into small blocks that are similar in subject and author. That is what Z-order and Hilbert clustering do with columns. And because new books arrive every day and get dropped on a returns trolley, someone has to periodically put them on the proper shelves, in order. That is compaction.

The analogy is imperfect in one important way: a library has one copy of each book, and moving books is cheap. A table's files are immutable, so "re-shelving" means rewriting files, which costs compute proportional to the data rewritten. Layout changes are therefore planned like small migrations, not done casually.

The levels of layout

From coarse to fine, a lake table's layout has four levels, and each one helps a different kind of query:

  1. Partitions — directories (or, in table formats, metadata groupings) by the value of a partition column such as date. Pruned by the planner before reading anything.
  2. Buckets (optional) — within a partition, a fixed number of files chosen by hashing a key. Used to join or aggregate without moving data.
  3. Files — each with per-column min/max statistics, either in its own footer or recorded in table-format metadata. Skipped by statistics when values are clustered.
  4. Row groups and pages inside files — the de2 level of skipping.

Keep this picture: partitions for the coarse filter everyone uses, ordering within partitions for the next most common filters, and file sizes kept healthy throughout.
body:
1. Hive-style partitioning and how pruning works

The convention most engines understand comes from Apache Hive: a partitioned table is a directory whose subdirectories are named column=value. A table partitioned by date has date=2026-10-07/, date=2026-10-08/ and so on, each containing Parquet files. The partition column is usually not stored in the files; its value comes from the directory name. A table can have several partition columns, nested: date=2026-10-08/country=DE/.

When a query arrives, the planner looks at its filter. If the filter constrains a partition column — WHERE date = '2026-10-08', WHERE date BETWEEN '2026-10-01' AND '2026-10-07' — it computes which partition values can match and lists or looks up only those directories. This is partition pruning, and its saving is total: the excluded partitions cost nothing, not even a listing. A catalog such as the Hive Metastore or AWS Glue stores the list of partitions with their locations, so the planner can find them without listing the bucket at all.

Worked example. An events table holds three years of data at 300 GB of Parquet per day: 1,095 partitions, about 330 TB. A query for one day prunes 1,094 partitions and reads at most 300 GB — 0.09% of the table — before any file statistics are consulted. A query for the last 7 days reads 2.1 TB. A query with no date filter (say, "all purchases by user 553 ever") reads all 330 TB unless something else skips data; partitioning does nothing for it.

Pruning has pitfalls that come from the partition column living outside the data. If the table is partitioned by date but a query filters on the event timestamp — WHERE ts >= '2026-10-08 00:00' — the planner does not know that ts and date are related, and prunes nothing; users must remember to add the redundant date filter. If a writer derives date from ts in a local time zone while readers assume UTC, rows near midnight sit in the "wrong" partition and date filters silently drop them. Partition values are strings in directory names, so a filter like WHERE month = 3 against directories named month=03 can mismatch. And filters wrapped in functions (WHERE year(date) = 2026) may or may not be pushed into pruning depending on the engine.

Iceberg's hidden partitioning fixes the first two problems (de4 covers the metadata that makes it possible). The table declares its partitions as a transform of a real column — PARTITIONED BY (day(ts)) — and the writer computes the partition value itself. A query filtering on ts is translated into a partition filter automatically, users never see or fill a separate date column, and the transform is defined in UTC once, for everyone.

2. Choosing partition columns: too few, too many

A good partition column has three properties. It is used in the filters of most queries (otherwise pruning rarely happens). It has low cardinality at the chosen granularity (a few hundred to a few thousand values over the table's life, not millions). And it leaves each partition large: Delta Lake's best-practice guide says you can partition by a column if you expect each partition to hold at least 1 GB, and advises against high-cardinality columns such as a user ID. For event and fact tables, the answer is nearly always a date; very large tables use hour; small tables (under a terabyte or so) often do best with no partitions at all and good file statistics.

Now the arithmetic of getting it wrong.

Too many. The same 300 GB/day table partitioned by date, country (200 values) and event_type (20 values) has up to 4,000 partitions a day and 1.46 million a year. The average partition holds 75 MB — already smaller than one good file. But real data is skewed: if the top 5 countries carry 60% of traffic, the other 195 countries share 120 GB across 3,900 partitions, about 31 MB each, and the long tail of small country-and-event combinations holds a few kilobytes. Then the write makes it worse. A Spark job with 500 tasks, where each task holds a random slice of the day's events, writes one file for every partition it has rows for — potentially 500 × 4,000 = 2 million files a day, most of them a few kilobytes. Every query on this table pays for listing and opening them, and the planner and catalog choke on the metadata.

Too few. The same table with no partitions at all: 330 TB in about 650,000 files of 512 MB. A query for one day must, at minimum, examine every file's statistics. In a plain Hive-style table that means opening every footer — hundreds of thousands of requests. In an Iceberg or Delta table the per-file min/max are already in the metadata, so if the files are written roughly in time order, the planner can skip all but the ~600 files of the right day from metadata alone; this is why table formats make partitioning less critical. But if files mix days (because late data was appended or files were compacted without regard to time), nothing can be skipped.

The middle. Partition by date only: 1,095 partitions of 300 GB, about 600 files each of 512 MB. Then use ordering within each day (sections 5–7) for the second and third most common filters. That is the default design for large event tables, and you should need a reason to depart from it.
